results.comment: 2:16:49 To those who are curious about the dolphins but don't want to Google. Basically for dolphins (and other sea mammals) getting stranded on beach is one of the worse nightmares. It has nothing to do with ability or inability to breathe, and more to do with moisture and mobility. Like imagine getting stranded in a desert. Scary because you don't know which way to go to get some shade and water before you die. And now imagine that you have an oasis clearly in your sight. Not a mirage, definitely real, only a short walk away. But your arms and legs are chopped off. So you have to suffer and more likely than not die within clear sight of salvation but utterly incapable of reaching it. This is why if a wild sea mammal "voluntarily" beaches itself, it is usually a sign that it is in a lot of pain and might actually be trying to self delete as a "better option". And in dolphin shows the dolphin jumping on a platform at the chandler's command is an impressive act.  So... Aside from an intended act of self deletion  the other likely way of how a dolphin might get into this situation is to caught in shallow beach when tide goes low. So being pushed into shallow water before low tide is an inherently scary thing for dolphins. And male dolphins use it. Groups of male dolphins would try to isolate a female dolphin and herd her dowards shallow waters with bites and headbutts, and force her to stay there unless she performs sexual acts with them. If translated to human, such behaviour would undoubtedly be classified as gang "grape".
